title: Model of Egyptian Nile Boat

image.credit: National Museum of Denmark; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: A small wooden model of a boat from ancient Egypt, with a crew of figures on board. The model is shown as an object on its own.

source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text via a page fetch (title, date, medium, collection, crew, tomb-model note, public-domain statement); the fetch was a machine summary, so a person should confirm the medium and collection on the page

context: A wooden model of a Nile boat from ancient Egypt, dated 2160 to 2130 BCE on arthistoryproject.com, which lists it with the National Museum of Denmark. The page says boats were central to life along the Nile and that models and paintings of boats were placed in tombs. It adds that this boat has a crew of nine.

descriptions.k: This is a little boat made long ago in Egypt. It is made of wood. People are on the boat. Point to the boat. Can you find the people? What do you think they are doing together?
descriptions.g12: This small wooden boat was made in ancient Egypt a very long time ago. It has a crew of nine people on board. The Nile river was very important to Egyptians, and boats helped people travel and carry things. Look closely at the boat and the crew. Where do you think this boat is going?
descriptions.g35: This is a model of a Nile boat from ancient Egypt, made about 2160 to 2130 BCE and listed with the National Museum of Denmark. The site says the boat is made of wood and has a crew of nine. Egyptians lived along the Nile, so boats were part of everyday life. Look closely at the crew and the shape of the boat. What jobs might each person on board have?
descriptions.g68: This wooden boat model is dated 2160 to 2130 BCE. The source page explains that life in Egypt centered on the Nile and that models and paintings of boats were included in tombs. Many model boats like this were made for tombs, though the page does not say where this one was found. It has a crew of nine. How might a small model tell us about real boats and daily life?
descriptions.g910: This wooden model of a Nile boat (2160 to 2130 BCE) is an example of a kind of object the source page says was placed in tombs, along with painted boats, so that the deceased could travel in the afterlife. Many model boats like this were made for tombs, but the page does not give this one's findspot. How does a model with a crew of nine act as both a record of river life and a funerary offering?
descriptions.g1112: Dated 2160 to 2130 BCE, this wooden model belongs to the Egyptian practice of placing boat models and boat paintings in tombs, which the source page links to the deceased's journey and possessions. Because the page does not give its findspot, any funerary use is an inference from the wider tradition. How should we read a small object that serves as both a reflection of a real river economy and a carefully made offering? Weigh the evidence and its limits.

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, date (2160-2130 BCE), medium (wood), collection (National Museum of Denmark), crew of nine, the note that boat models were placed in tombs, the tag Boats and the public-domain statement were read from a fetch of the arthistoryproject.com page; the assigning brief said the page gave no medium or collection, so a person should confirm those two facts on the page. Sensitive aspect for the reviewer: the model has a funerary/tomb context. Descriptions for K to grade 5 focus on the boat, wood, shape and crew and do not mention tombs or death; the tomb and afterlife context is stated factually and respectfully only from grade 6 up, and findspot claims are hedged because the page gives none. The image file has not been viewed; a person should view it and confirm it before release. Movement label First Intermediate Period is inferred from the date 2160-2130 BCE and should be checked.

teacherNote.context: A wooden model of a Nile boat with a crew of nine, dated 2160 to 2130 BCE on arthistoryproject.com, which lists it with the National Museum of Denmark. The page says models and paintings of boats were placed in tombs; the page gives no findspot for this model.
directions: Have younger students build a simple boat from paper or craft sticks and decide who would travel on it and why.
Ask older students to compare what a model can and cannot tell us about a real object from the past.
Discuss respectfully how the Egyptians' ideas about tombs and the afterlife shaped the objects they made, noting which points come from the page and which are general history.
